title: Chapter 42 — The Whiteness of the Whale
paragraphs: What the white whale meant to Ahab has been hinted at. What he was to me, at times, remains unsaid.

Beyond the more obvious fears that Moby Dick could stir in any man's soul, there was another thought — or rather a vague, nameless horror about him — that sometimes overpowered everything else with its intensity. Yet it was so mystical, so nearly impossible to put into words, that I almost despair of making it comprehensible. It was the whiteness of the whale that appalled me above all things. But how can I hope to explain myself here? And yet, in some dim, fumbling way, explain myself I must, or all these chapters will have been for nothing.

In many natural objects, whiteness refines and enhances beauty, as if imparting some special virtue of its own — as in marbles, japonicas, and pearls. Various nations have in some way recognized a certain royal preeminence in this color. The barbaric, grand old kings of Pegu placed the title "Lord of the White Elephants" above all their other grandiloquent titles of dominion. The modern kings of Siam unfurled the same snow-white animal on their royal standard. The Hanoverian flag bore the single figure of a snow-white charger. The great Austrian Empire, Caesarian, heir to overlording Rome, took the same imperial hue for its imperial color. This preeminence applies to the human race itself, giving the white man ideal mastership over every dusky tribe. Beyond all this, whiteness has even been made a sign of gladness — among the Romans, a white stone marked a joyful day. In other human sympathies and symbols, this same color is made the emblem of many touching, noble things: the innocence of brides, the kindliness of old age. Among the Red Men of America, the gift of the white belt of wampum was the deepest pledge of honor. In many lands, whiteness represents the majesty of Justice in the judge's ermine, and adds to the daily grandeur of kings and queens drawn by milk-white steeds. Even in the higher mysteries of the most august religions, it has been made the symbol of divine spotlessness and power. The Persian fire worshippers held the white forked flame the holiest on the altar. In the Greek mythologies, great Jove himself was made incarnate in a snow-white bull. Among the noble Iroquois, the midwinter sacrifice of the sacred White Dog was by far the holiest festival of their theology — that spotless, faithful creature being held the purest envoy they could send to the Great Spirit with the yearly news of their own faithfulness. Directly from the Latin word for white, all Christian priests derive the name of one part of their sacred vestments — the alb, or tunic, worn beneath the cassock. Among the holy ceremonies of the Romish faith, white is specially used in celebrating the Passion of our Lord. In the Vision of St. John, white robes are given to the redeemed, and the twenty-four elders stand clothed in white before the great white throne, and the Holy One who sits there is white like wool. Yet for all these accumulated associations with whatever is sweet, honorable, and sublime, there still lurks something elusive in the innermost idea of this color that strikes more panic into the soul than the redness that frightens us in blood.

It is this elusive quality that causes the thought of whiteness, when separated from kinder associations and joined to any object terrible in itself, to heighten that terror to its furthest limits. Consider the white bear of the poles and the white shark of the tropics. What but their smooth, flaky whiteness makes them the transcendent horrors they are? It is that ghastly whiteness that gives such an abhorrent mildness, even more loathsome than terrifying, to the dumb gloating of their look. So that not even the fierce-fanged tiger in his heraldic coat can so stagger courage as the white-shrouded bear or shark.*

*With reference to the polar bear, it may possibly be argued by anyone who would like to go still deeper into this matter that it is not the whiteness, considered by itself, that heightens the intolerable hideousness of that beast. For, analyzed, that heightened hideousness, it might be said, only arises from the fact that the irresponsible ferociousness of the creature is dressed in the fleece of heavenly innocence and love; and so, by bringing together two such opposite emotions in our minds, the polar bear frightens us with so unnatural a contrast. But even assuming all this to be true, if it were not for the whiteness, you would not have that intensified terror.

As for the white shark, the white gliding ghostliness of that creature at rest, when seen in its ordinary moods, strangely matches the same quality in the polar quadruped. The French hit off this peculiarity most vividly in the name they give that fish. The Romish mass for the dead begins with "Requiem eternam" (eternal rest), from which "Requiem" names the mass itself and any other funeral music. Now, in allusion to the white, silent stillness of death in this shark, and the mild deadliness of his habits, the French call him Requin.

Think of the albatross. Where do those clouds of spiritual wonder and pale dread come from, in which that white phantom sails in every imagination? It was not Coleridge who first cast that spell, but God's great, unflattering poet laureate, Nature.*

*I remember the first albatross I ever saw. It was during a prolonged gale, in waters close to the Antarctic seas. From my morning watch below, I climbed up to the overclouded deck. There, dashed down upon the main hatches, I saw a regal, feathery thing of unspotted whiteness, with a hooked, Roman bill, sublime. At intervals it arched out its vast archangel wings, as if to embrace some holy ark. Wondrous flutterings and throbbings shook it. Though its body was unharmed, it uttered cries like some king's ghost in supernatural distress. Through its inexpressible, strange eyes, I thought I peered into secrets that took hold of God. Like Abraham before the angels, I bowed myself. The white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those forever-exiled waters I had lost the miserable, warping memories of traditions and of towns. Long I gazed at that prodigy of plumage. I cannot tell — I can only hint at — the things that darted through me then. But at last I came to myself, and turning, asked a sailor what bird this was. A goney, he replied. Goney! I had never heard that name before. Is it conceivable that this glorious thing is utterly unknown to men ashore? Never! But some time afterward I learned that "goney" was a seaman's name for the albatross. So by no possibility could Coleridge's wild Rhyme have had anything to do with those mystical impressions of mine when I saw that bird on our deck. For I had not then read the Rhyme, nor did I know the bird to be an albatross. Yet in saying this, I only indirectly polish a little brighter the noble merit of the poem and the poet.

I maintain, then, that the secret of the spell lurks chiefly in the bird's wondrous bodily whiteness. This truth is all the more evident from the fact that, by a contradiction in terms, there are birds called gray albatrosses. These I have often seen, but never with such emotions as when I beheld the Antarctic fowl.

But how had the mystic thing been caught? Don't breathe a word, and I will tell you: with a treacherous hook and line, as the bird floated on the sea. At last the Captain made a postman of it, tying a lettered leather tag around its neck with the ship's time and place, and then letting it escape. But I have no doubt that the leather tag, meant for man, was taken off in Heaven, when the white bird flew up to join the wing-folding, the invoking, and adoring cherubim!

Most famous in our Western annals and Indian traditions is the White Steed of the Prairies — a magnificent milk-white charger, large-eyed, small-headed, broad-chested, with the dignity of a thousand monarchs in his lofty, scornful bearing. He was the elected Xerxes of vast herds of wild horses, whose pastures in those days were fenced only by the Rocky Mountains and the Alleghenies. At their flaming head he trooped westward like that chosen star which every evening leads on the hosts of light. The flashing cascade of his mane and the curving comet of his tail decked him in trappings more resplendent than gold- and silver-beaters could have furnished. He was a most imperial and archangelic apparition of that unfallen western world, which to the eyes of the old trappers and hunters revived the glories of those primeval times when Adam walked majestic as a god, bluff-browed and fearless as this mighty steed. Whether marching among his aides and marshals at the front of countless columns that streamed endlessly over the plains like an Ohio, or whether, with his subjects browsing all around him to the horizon, he reviewed them at a gallop, his warm nostrils reddening through his cool milkiness — in whatever aspect he presented himself, he was always an object of trembling reverence and awe to the bravest Indians. Nor can it be questioned, from what stands on legendary record of this noble horse, that it was chiefly his spiritual whiteness that so clothed him with divineness; and that this divineness had something in it which, though commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror.
But there are other cases where whiteness loses all that added strange glory it possesses in the White Steed and the Albatross.

What is it about the albino man that so particularly repels and often shocks the eye, so that he is sometimes despised by his own family? It is the whiteness that covers him, the very thing expressed by his name. The albino is as well-built as other men — he has no real deformity — and yet this all-pervading whiteness makes him more strangely hideous than the ugliest abortion (a misshapen, monstrous birth). Why should this be?

Nor, in quite different aspects, does Nature, in her least tangible but no less malicious workings, fail to enlist this crowning attribute of the terrible among her forces. From its snowy appearance, the gauntleted ghost of the Southern Seas has been named the White Squall. Nor, in some historical cases, has the art of human malice left out so potent an ally. How wildly it heightens the effect of that passage in Froissart, when, masked in the snowy symbol of their faction, the desperate White Hoods of Ghent murder their bailiff in the marketplace!

In certain things, the common inherited experience of all humanity bears witness to the supernatural quality of this color. It can hardly be doubted that the one visible quality in the appearance of the dead that most horrifies the viewer is the marble paleness lingering there — as if that pallor were as much the mark of terror in the next world as it is of mortal fear in this one. From the pallor of the dead, we borrow the color of the shroud we wrap them in. Even in our superstitions we throw the same snowy cloak around our ghosts — all phantoms rise in a milk-white fog. And while these terrors grip us, let us add that even the king of terrors himself, as portrayed by the evangelist, rides on a pale horse.

Therefore, whatever grand or gracious thing a person may symbolize through whiteness in other moods, no one can deny that in its deepest, most idealized meaning, it summons a peculiar specter to the soul.

But though this point is settled beyond dispute, how can any mortal account for it? To analyze it would seem impossible. Can we, then, by citing some of those cases where this thing of whiteness — though for the time mostly or entirely stripped of all direct associations that might lend it anything fearful — is nevertheless found to work the same spell on us, however modified, hope to stumble upon some clue that leads us to the hidden cause we seek?

Let's try. But in a matter like this, subtlety speaks to subtlety, and without imagination nobody can follow anyone else into these halls. And though no doubt at least some of the imaginative impressions I am about to present may have been shared by most people, perhaps few were fully aware of them at the time, and so they may not be able to call them up now.

Why does the bare mention of Whitsuntide (the church season of Pentecost), to the man of untrained imagination who happens to be only loosely acquainted with the particular character of the day, marshal in his fancy such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-pacing pilgrims, downcast and hooded with new-fallen snow? Or why, to the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the Middle American States, does the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun call up such an eyeless statue in the soul?

Or what is it — apart from the traditions of dungeoned warriors and kings, which will not wholly account for it — that makes the White Tower of London strike the imagination of an untraveled American so much more strongly than those other storied structures, its neighbors, the Byward Tower, or even the Bloody Tower? And those sublimer towers, the White Mountains of New Hampshire — why, in certain moods, does such a gigantic ghostliness come over the soul at the bare mention of that name, while the thought of Virginia's Blue Ridge is full of a soft, dewy, distant dreaminess? Or why, regardless of all latitudes and longitudes, does the name of the White Sea cast such a spectral spell over the imagination, while that of the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long, lacquered, mild afternoons on the waves, followed by the gaudiest yet sleepiest of sunsets? Or, to choose a wholly insubstantial example, addressed purely to the imagination, why, in reading the old fairy tales of Central Europe, does "the tall pale man" of the Harz forests, whose changeless pallor glides without a rustle through the green of the groves — why is this phantom more terrible than all the whooping imps of the Blocksberg?

It is not entirely the memory of her cathedral-toppling earthquakes, nor the stampedes of her frantic seas, nor the tearlessness of arid skies that never rain, nor the sight of her wide field of leaning spires, wrenched copestones, and crosses all adroop (like the tilted yards of anchored fleets), and her suburban avenues of house-walls lying over upon one another like a tossed pack of cards — it is not these things alone that make tearless Lima the strangest, saddest city you can see. For Lima has taken the white veil, and there is a higher horror in this whiteness of her woe. Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins forever new. It does not admit the cheerful greenness of complete decay. It spreads over her broken ramparts the rigid pallor of a stroke that fixes its own distortions.

I know that to ordinary perception, whiteness is not admitted to be the prime agent in heightening the terror of things already terrible. Nor does the unimaginative mind find any terror in those sights whose awfulness, to another mind, consists almost entirely in this one quality — especially when displayed in any form approaching silence or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be clarified by the following examples.

First: The sailor, when approaching foreign coasts, if he hears the roar of breakers at night, snaps to alertness and feels just enough fear to sharpen all his senses. But under exactly the same conditions, let him be called from his hammock to see his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness — as if herds of combed white bears were swimming around him from encircling headlands — and he feels a silent, superstitious dread. The shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is as horrible to him as a real ghost. In vain the sounding lead assures him he is still in deep water. Heart and helm both fail him. He never rests until blue water is beneath him again. Yet where is the sailor who will tell you, "Sir, it was not so much the fear of hitting hidden rocks as the fear of that hideous whiteness that shook me"?

Second: To the native Indian of Peru, the continual sight of the snow-howdahed Andes (their peaks capped with snow like the canopied seat on an elephant's back) conveys nothing of dread, except perhaps in merely imagining the eternal frozen desolation that reigns at such vast heights, and the natural thought of how fearful it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same is true of the backwoodsman of the West, who views with comparative indifference a boundless prairie sheeted with driven snow, with no shadow of tree or twig to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas, where at times, by some infernal sleight of hand in the powers of frost and air, he — shivering and half shipwrecked — instead of seeing rainbows that speak hope and comfort to his misery, sees what looks like a boundless churchyard grinning at him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.
But you say: "I think this white-lead chapter about whiteness is just a white flag hung out by a cowardly soul. You are giving in to a fit of the blues, Ishmael."

Tell me, then — why does a strong young colt, born in some peaceful Vermont valley, far from all predators — why is it that on the sunniest day, if you shake a fresh buffalo hide behind him so he cannot even see it but only smells its wild animal musk — why will he bolt, snort, and paw the ground in frenzy with bulging eyes? He has no memory of being attacked by wild creatures in his green northern home. The strange muskiness cannot remind him of any past danger. What does this New England colt know of the black bison herds of distant Oregon?

Nothing. But here you see, even in a speechless animal, the instinct of knowing the demonic forces in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, when he smells that savage musk, the charging, goring bison herds are as real to him as they are to the abandoned wild foal on the prairies, which at this very moment they may be trampling into dust.

So it is: the muffled rollings of a milky sea, the bleak rustlings of the festooned frosts of mountains, the desolate shiftings of the windrowed snows of prairies — all these are to Ishmael what the shaking of that buffalo robe is to the frightened colt!

Neither the colt nor I knows where the nameless things lie of which the mystic sign gives such hints; yet for me, as for the colt, those things must exist somewhere. Though in many ways this visible world seems to have been made in love, the invisible spheres were made in fright.

But we have not yet solved the spell of this whiteness or learned why it appeals with such power to the soul. And stranger still, far more ominous — why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaningful symbol of spiritual things, the very veil of the Christian's God, and yet at the same time the intensifying agent in things most appalling to humanity.

Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and so stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation when we gaze into the white depths of the Milky Way? Or is it that whiteness, in its essence, is not so much a color as the visible absence of color, and at the same time the concrete of all colors? Is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows — a colorless all-color of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues — every stately or lovely emblazoning, the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods, yes, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls — all these are only subtle deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from outside; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we go further and consider that the mystical cosmetic that produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, forever remains white or colorless in itself, and if it acted upon matter without a medium, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge — pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper. And like willful travelers in Lapland who refuse to wear colored and coloring glasses over their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps the whole prospect around him. And of all these things the albino whale was the symbol. Do you wonder, then, at the fiery hunt?
